svg.text: Deep dive 2 — NFR4: data is toxic sludge (storage budget + the 30-day purge)
we only do math when the number changes a decision — here it sizes the DB and justifies the cleanup job
1B users × 100 messages/day = 100B messages/day × 1 KB cap = 100 TB/day
IF we kept everything × 30 days that would balloon — but most messages are ACKed and deleted the same second,
so the live database ends up around a few hundred TB. Large but ordinary — modern systems do this daily.
the number isn't the point — the DERIVATION is: units → daily rate → what's deleted early.
Cleanup service (cron) — delete early, delete often
① messages table carries timestamp (server-stamped). Add a secondary index on it →
DELETE rows where ts < now − 30 days. Hard guarantee, no per-row bookkeeping.
② inbox rows die on ACK (they're the delivery state). Add a timestamp there too, so
forgotten/stale undelivered rows are purged the same way.
③ when the LAST inbox row for a message is deleted, delete the message row as well
(everyone has it → nobody needs the server copy).
race conditions exist — the 30-day guard rail absorbs them: worst case we keep an extra copy for a day. harmless.
Why WhatsApp is the right product for aggressive deletion
· privacy liability is expensive (Meta pays dearly when it gets this wrong) — the server should hold plaintext as little as possible.
· messages are E2E-encrypted anyway: "the ideal is to either delete it, or encrypt it so even we can't read it" (Stefan, verbatim).
bonus tie-in: this is the same muscle as ticketmaster's TTL lock and the 30-day media expiry from HLD v3.
